title: Why governance: policies, procedures & delegated authority
blurb: Explain why projects need policies, regulations, functions, processes, procedures and delegated responsibilities, and what goes wrong without them.
question: A water company is replacing 40 km of pipeline. The project must follow the company's procurement policy, environmental regulations, a standard change control process and agreed spending limits for each manager. Why does the project need each of these, and what would happen without them?

teach.h: Governance: who decides, by what rules
teach.body: Project governance is the framework of authority and accountability that directs and controls a project, aligned with the organisation's own practices. It is built from six aspects: policies, regulations, functions, processes, procedures and delegated responsibilities. Plain English: governance says who is allowed to decide what, which rules must be followed, who checks, and how things are done, so that money and risk are controlled and everyone can trust the project.

teach.h: Each aspect, with an example and its purpose
head: Aspect
Example
Why it is needed
rows: Procurement policy: tender above a set value
How to raise a change request
Everyone does a task the same way
PM may approve spend up to a limit

teach.caption: A policy is the organisation's own rule; a regulation is imposed from outside and cannot be waived by the organisation.

teach.body: Together the six aspects give five things a project cannot do without. ACCOUNTABILITY: every decision has a named owner. CONSISTENCY: projects are run and reported the same way, so they can be compared. COMPLIANCE: legal duties and internal rules are met. CONTROL OF RISK AND MONEY: spending and risk-taking stay within agreed limits. CONFIDENCE: sponsors, boards, regulators and funders can trust what they are told. Governance should be scaled to the project, but never skipped.

Authority is delegated down the governance structure, each level with defined limits called tolerances: the board to the sponsor, the sponsor to the project manager, the project manager to team leaders. Inside those limits each person decides without asking, which keeps work moving. Anything forecast beyond a limit is escalated to the level that set it. Delegation without limits loses control; limits without delegation create bottlenecks where every small decision waits for a senior signature.

The procurement POLICY means pipe supply is competitively tendered. Environmental REGULATIONS require permits before work near rivers. The legal and finance FUNCTIONS review contracts and payments; the PMO checks reports. The change control PROCESS handles route changes, and a PROCEDURE explains exactly how to raise one. DELEGATED responsibilities let the PM approve variations up to an agreed limit. When a river crossing needs an unplanned tunnel beyond that limit, the PM escalates it to the sponsor.

teach.text: Don't mix them up. A POLICY is the organisation's own rule; a REGULATION is external (law or industry) and cannot be waived internally. A PROCESS is the repeatable sequence of activities (change control); a PROCEDURE is the detailed instructions for carrying out one task within it (how to fill in the change request).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the aspect and say what it is in one line (policy, regulation, function, process, procedure, delegated responsibility).
Give a concrete example from the scenario.
Explain the benefit: accountability, consistency, compliance, control or confidence.
State the consequence of missing it (unauthorised spend, fines, slow decisions).
Governance = the framework of authority and accountability for a project.
Six aspects: policies, regulations, functions, processes, procedures, delegated responsibilities.
Policies are internal rules; regulations are external and must be complied with.
Processes are repeatable sequences; procedures are detailed task instructions.
Benefits: accountability, consistency, compliance, control of risk and money, confidence.

summary: You can now explain what each of the six aspects of project governance is, give an example of each, and explain why they are needed. You can also describe what goes wrong when governance is missing or badly delegated.

A.q: A retailer requires every purchase above a set value to be competitively tendered. Which aspect of governance is this?
A.why: This is the organisation's own rule about how it buys: a policy.

whyNot.0: A regulation is imposed externally, by law or an industry body.
whyNot.1: A procedure gives step-by-step instructions for a task, not the rule itself.
whyNot.3: A function is a part of the organisation, such as finance or procurement.

A.q: A construction project must comply with the CDM Regulations 2015. Which aspect of governance does this represent?
A.why: CDM 2015 is law imposed from outside the organisation: a regulation.

whyNot.1: A policy is the organisation's own rule, which it could change; CDM cannot be waived.
whyNot.2: Delegated responsibility is about authority levels, not legal duties.
whyNot.3: A process is an internal way of working, though processes help meet the regulation.

A.q: Why does project governance need DELEGATED responsibilities?
options: So all decisions go to the board
So the PMO can approve every spend
So users can sign off the budget
So each level knows its limits
A.why: Delegation with limits lets each level decide within its authority and escalate beyond it, keeping both control and pace.

whyNot.0: Sending every decision to the board creates bottlenecks; delegation prevents this.
whyNot.1: A PMO supports governance; it does not hold all spending authority.
whyNot.2: Budget approval sits with the sponsor and board, not users.

options: A law the organisation must obey
A department such as legal or HR
The limit on what a manager may spend
B.why: A procedure is the detailed set of instructions for carrying out one task, such as raising a change request.

whyNot.0: A law the organisation must obey is a regulation.
whyNot.2: A department such as legal or HR is a function.
whyNot.3: A spending limit is part of delegated responsibilities.

B.q: Before a major supply contract is signed, it is reviewed by the legal and finance departments. Which aspect of governance is at work?
B.why: Legal and finance are organisational functions that bring specialist expertise and independent checks into the project's governance.

whyNot.0: A policy may require the review, but the departments doing it are functions.
whyNot.1: Regulations are external rules, not internal departments.
whyNot.2: A procedure describes how a task is done, not who in the organisation checks it.

B.q: A bank makes all its projects use the same risk and change control processes. What is the MAIN benefit?
options: No need for a sponsor on small projects
Fewer regulations apply to its projects
Projects need no tolerances or limits
B.why: Common processes mean every project is controlled and reported the same way, so the board can compare them and trust the information.

whyNot.1: Every project still needs a sponsor, whatever processes it uses.
whyNot.2: Regulations apply regardless of internal processes.
whyNot.3: Processes work alongside tolerances; they do not replace them.

C.q: A charity's auditors find that two project managers committed funds that nobody had authorised, because no one knew who could approve what. Which governance aspect MOST directly fixes this?
C.why: The failure is unclear authority. Delegated responsibilities with defined limits say who may approve what, and when to escalate.

whyNot.0: Regulations are external; the gap is internal authority.
whyNot.1: A sustainability policy does not define who may approve spending.
whyNot.3: Better reporting may reveal the problem but doesn't define approval authority.

C.q: Which TWO are set INSIDE the organisation rather than imposed from outside? 1. Policies  2. Regulations  3. Procedures  4. Data protection law
C.why: Policies and procedures are the organisation's own; regulations and laws such as data protection are external.

C.q: The founder of a fast-growing start-up says governance is 'just bureaucracy that slows us down'. Which is the BEST response?
options: Agreed: governance is only for public bodies
Agreed: skip it until there's a problem
Governance is only needed by regulators
Scaled governance gives control and trust
C.why: Governance gives accountability, compliance, control of risk and money, and confidence for investors. It should be scaled to the project, not skipped.

whyNot.0: Every organisation spending money on change needs governance, not just public bodies.
whyNot.1: Waiting for a problem means losing control; governance prevents problems as well as handling them.
whyNot.2: Governance serves the organisation's own sponsors, boards and investors, not only regulators.

reteach.title: Running a school trip
reteach.question: A school is taking 60 pupils to France. What are the policies, regulations, functions, processes, procedures and delegated responsibilities?

blocks.body: The school's trips POLICY sets staff-to-pupil ratios. REGULATIONS include safeguarding law and passport rules. FUNCTIONS such as the finance office and the head's office check payments and risk assessments. The trip approval PROCESS runs from proposal to sign-off; the PROCEDURE for a medical form says exactly how to fill it in. DELEGATED responsibility lets the trip leader spend up to an agreed amount on the day; anything bigger is a call to the head.

head: School trip
Governance aspect
rows: How to complete a medical form

blocks.text: The school can rewrite its own ratio policy, but it cannot rewrite safeguarding law. That is the policy versus regulation difference in one line.

explain.body: Policies are the organisation's own rules (procurement, risk, health and safety, sustainability). Regulations are external legal or industry rules (CDM 2015, UK GDPR, Bribery Act 2010). Both must be followed; only policies can be changed by the organisation.

test.q: Which statement about regulations is correct?
options: They are external rules to be obeyed
They can be waived by the project sponsor
They are written by the project's own PMO
They apply only to public sector projects
test.why: Regulations are imposed from outside (law or industry bodies) and must be complied with.

whyNot.1: A sponsor cannot waive the law.
whyNot.2: A PMO writes internal standards and templates, not regulations.
whyNot.3: Regulations such as UK GDPR and health and safety law apply in all sectors.

explain.body: Functions are parts of the organisation that support and check projects: finance, legal, HR, procurement, health and safety and the PMO. They bring specialist expertise and an independent view, so the project does not mark its own homework.

test.q: Why are functions such as finance and legal part of project governance?
options: They replace the need for a sponsor
They manage the project day to day
They decide which benefits to claim
test.why: Functions bring specialist expertise and an independent check on contracts, money, people and compliance.

whyNot.0: Every project still needs a sponsor.
whyNot.1: Day-to-day management is the project manager's job.
whyNot.3: Benefits are set in the business case owned by the sponsor.

explain.body: A process is a repeatable sequence of activities, such as change control or risk management. A procedure is the detailed instruction for carrying out one task within it. Both make work consistent and predictable across projects.

steps.label: Procedure
steps.sub: Exactly how to complete the request form

test.q: A team uses a defined sequence of steps to assess and approve every change. What is this sequence an example of?
test.why: A repeatable sequence of activities such as change control is a process.

whyNot.0: A regulation is an external rule, not an internal sequence of steps.
whyNot.2: A tolerance is a permitted deviation, delegated to a role.
whyNot.3: A function is a department such as finance or legal.

explain.body: Authority passes down from the board to the sponsor, project manager and team leaders, each with tolerances. Inside the limits they decide; beyond them they escalate. This keeps decisions fast but controlled.

explain.caption: Authority is delegated down; issues beyond a limit are escalated back up.

test.q: What is the MAIN risk if authority is NOT delegated to the project manager?
options: Decisions are made with no limits at all
Regulations stop applying to the project
Small decisions wait for senior sign-off
The PMO takes over the sponsor's role
test.why: Without delegation every decision waits for a senior signature, creating bottlenecks and slowing delivery.

whyNot.0: Unlimited decisions is the risk of delegation WITHOUT limits, the opposite problem.
whyNot.3: Lack of delegation doesn't move the sponsor's role to the PMO.
